item.title: Efficient Recovery of Latent Coordinate Structure from Sparse Observations of the Hypercube
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Rares-Darius Buhai, Davide Mazzali, Weronika Wrzos-Kaminska

Recovering latent geometric structure from graph observations is a well-studied problem in statistical inference. Kapralov, Trevisan, and Wrzos-Kaminska (2026) introduced the problem of recovering the coordinate structure of the Boolean hypercube from a small random sample of its edges. More specifically, there are $n=2^d$ vertices, each corresponding to a distinct "feature" vector in $\{\pm 1\}^d$. Between each pair whose feature vectors are at Hamming distance one, an edge is observed independently with probability $p$. As long as the expected degree $pd$ is $\gtrsim \log d = \log \log n$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that, given only the graph of observed edges, correctly recovers the entire feature vector of all but a vanishing fraction of vertices. This matches the information-theoretic guarantee of Kapralov, Trevisan, and Wrzos-Kaminska in polynomial rather than exponential time, resolving the algorithmic question left open by their work. Our algorithm combines a degree-$4$ sum-of-squares certificate for the structure of balanced near-minimum cuts with a rounding scheme originally developed for tensor decomposition by Ma, Shi, and Steurer (2016). The analysis relies on two novel ingredients: a sum-of-squares version of the Friedgut-Kalai-Naor theorem in Boolean Fourier analysis and a spectral concentration result for the observed subgraph of the hypercube. Finally, we provide a justification for why higher-degree sum-of-squares might be needed by showing a limitation of the basic SDP relaxation of this problem.

item.title: Faster Planar Graph Algorithms for Connectivity Problems via Meanders
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Susanna Caroppo, Giordano Da Lozzo, Giuseppe Di Battista, Jevgēnijs Vihrovs

In this paper, we refine the dynamic programming framework based on the sphere cut decomposition designed by Dorn, Penninkx, Bodlaender, and Fomin (ESA 2005) to obtain faster subexponential algorithms for connectivity problems on planar graphs. We investigate the relationship between these problems and meanders, which are simple closed planar loops that intersect a fixed line in a given number of points. By combining dynamic programming with techniques from meandric system analysis and the use of fast matrix multiplication by Dorn (ESA 2006), we obtain improved algorithms for planar connectivity problems. We show that the number of meanders on $2n$ crossings $M_n$ is $\mathcal O^*(12.806^n)$, which improves the previous upper bound of $\mathcal O^*(12.901^n)$ by Albert and Paterson (FPSAC 2004). This then gives the best-known classical upper bounds on the deterministic time complexity of several planar graph problems with polynomially-bounded weights, namely $\mathcal O(2^{5.543\sqrt n})$ for the Planar Travelling Salesman problem, $\mathcal O(2^{5.796\sqrt n})$ for Planar Longest Cycle/Path, $\mathcal O(2^{8.251\sqrt n})$ for Planar Connected Dominating Set and $\mathcal O(2^{8.037\sqrt n})$ for Planar Steiner Tree. Notably, this leads to the best-known deterministic complexity $\mathcal O(2^{5.543\sqrt{n}})$ for the Planar Hamiltonian Cycle problem.

item.title: Parallel Edge Ranking of Trees
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Jeff Giliberti, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Changki Yun

In this work, we prove that computing the edge ranking of a tree in parallel is P-Complete. An optimal tree edge ranking assigns positive integer ranks to the edges such that any two edges with the same rank are separated by an edge of higher rank, while minimizing the highest rank. Tree edge ranking abstracts several classical problems such as parallel assembly in manufacturing, minimum-height dendrograms, reversible pebble game and edge-query binary search on trees. Its parallel complexity remained open for over thirty years, since the seminal work of de la Torre, Greenlaw, and Sch{ä}ffer [SODA'93], and was listed as an open problem in the book Limits to Parallel Computation by Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo [1995]. We prove that deciding whether a tree has edge ranking at most $K$ is P-Complete, already for trees of diameter six. Our reduction is from NOR-CVP and simulates a greedy procedure underlying known sequential approaches. Despite ruling out NC algorithms, we prove that this hardness barrier can be bypassed in the well-known model of Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) with strongly sublinear local memory, showing that $O(\log n)$ MPC rounds suffice to solve the hard tree-edge ranking instances used to prove P-Completeness. Specifically, we present a deterministic MPC algorithm that computes an optimal edge ranking of an $n$-vertex tree of diameter $D$ in $O(\log D+\log\log n)$ rounds with $O(n^{3/4}D^{1/4})$ local memory. Our algorithm circumvents the linear-memory barrier by compressing the information required to produce a lexicographically minimal ranking from subtree merges. Overall, this result reinforces the strict separation between NC and what can be computed efficiently in MPC.

item.title: $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ Lower Bounds for Dynamic Graph Problems
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Young Kun Ko

We prove an $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ unconditional lower bound on the maximum of the query time and update time for dynamic data structures supporting reachability queries in $n$-node directed acyclic graphs under edge insertions. This improves the $\widetildeΩ(\log^{3/2} n)$ lower bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025], and matches the strongest lower bound known for any dynamic problem. The same bound holds for incremental undirected shortest paths and subgraph connectivity. To prove it, we bring the recent framework of Ko [FOCS 2026], which gave this bound for Pătraşcu's multiphase problem with Inner Product, to the multiphase problem with Disjointness. Our main technical contribution is to show that verification in Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication game makes a one-sided corruption bound suffice in place of discrepancy, which Disjointness lacks.

item.title: TCS, AI, and the Adults in the Room
item.description:
Filter match: person: sepehr assadi

Guest Post by Clément Canonne, PDF version

When I was a kid, my parents looked in control. Even when bad things happened, they knew what to do, what to say, told us not to worry, did the things adults do to make things work out, and things did work out.

Now that I am less of a kid, I realize that they were not (always) in control. When bad things happened, they took responsibility to reclaim agency. They put on an adult face, figured out what to say, told us not to worry, and then silently did whatever they could so that things worked out. They just did their best, and we did not know, and we did not have to worry.

And now, for something completely different.

AI. We’re currently facing a rather obvious crisis, “what happens when a self-proclaimed unstoppable force meets a historically very slow-moving object.” I’m not going to detail what you probably all have witnessed and seen evolve over what feels like an eternity and the blink of an eye, but we need to reevaluate many things. Bad things are happening.1 We are not in control. We do not really know what to do. But, as Omer Reingold wrote so well,2 if you are a senior academic or industry researcher, snap out of it:

“Contemplating the end of your profession from the relative comfort of an established, tenured career is a privilege, and it comes with responsibilities. Senior academics are not merely individual researchers; we are stewards of our field, and we owe our junior colleagues active leadership rather than abandonment.”

Perhaps more bluntly, and less eloquently than Omer put it: we “senior academics” are supposed to be the adults. Complacency, doom-erism, and generally navel-gazing, while tempting, are unacceptable, counter-productive, and frankly unbecoming: we have a duty of care to our students, mentees, our community.

We need to put on an adult face, figure out what to say to them, tell them not to worry, and then silently do whatever we can so that things work out for them.

That’s not to say we should lie! It is, again, about taking responsibility, and coming up with a plan and solutions: letting others know that we are here for them, and that they can count on us. So I’ll outline some thoughts here about what to do now: mostly two. (1) We must find out what we want to fight for and preserve. (2) One concrete action to take.

What’s below is mostly targeted at “senior people,” but feel free to read on if you are junior – Ph.D., postdoc, untenured faculty or (good god!) born after The Dark Knight was released in theaters.

(1) We need to figure out what our values are, our justification, and we need to do it yesterday.

So let’s all take a break from freaking out about the latest longstanding conjecture whose resolution just appeared on the arXiv, and think about what it means to be doing Theoretical Computer Science, what our social mandate is, why we are doing what we are doing and why society has been paying us (quite well, actually) to do so.

  • Is it to create knowledge, investigate fundamental questions for the very sake of it?

  • Is is to disseminate knowledge, practical and/or abstract, to society?

  • Is it to equip students, undergraduate and postgraduate, with a specific set of skills, to view and navigate the world with a computational mindset?

  • Is it to solve problems relevant to society and to industry, with the bulk of our research being in some sense a “side quest” in support of this goal?

  • …

  • Is it to keep us at arms’ length, and prevent a bunch of people with an unhealthy knack for solving math puzzles from doing much worse things, like building an underground lair or starting a financial crisis?

Or is it something else entirely? Or a combination of all of the above? We may all have slightly different views on this, and I don’t have definite answers, but we should all be thinking about it (or, rather, we should all already have been thinking about it). Thankfully, we don’t have to start from nothing, because the giants whose shoulders we are camping on did give it some thought, and still are (see,  [@AhoJKKMPP96], and the response [@GoldreichW96] for a start3): but we must, starting from there, form our own opinions, decide what our values are, why we do what we do, and why society should give us a license to do so. We won’t know what to do, can’t figure out what to say, unless we know why we do what we do and what we stand for as a community.

Putting my money where my mouth is, here are some of my own views. 4

  1. We are meant to create knowledge, build theories, and new ways to look at things This involves many different aspects, among which “proving theorems” is at best the tip of the iceberg (unfortunately, as for icebergs, this is also usually the only one people notice). We should explore what “computation” means and could mean, driven by curiosity, yes, but also because it reveals new understanding which can shape the way we, and down the line many others, think. I see the concept of reduction between problems and the shift in thinking associated with it as one of the most beautiful and influential contributions of TCS: one which not only influenced (deeply) the theory of computation, algorithms, and complexity, but also one we teach our students, and might change the lens through which they view other aspects of their life.

  2. We are not mathematically-inclined tech consultants. As theoretical computer scientists, our reason d’être is not to solve problems from or for industry, or to only worry about current or near-future practical tasks they want to solve.5 This is not to say we shouldn’t think about these problems as a source of potentially interesting research questions. Interesting algorithmic questions can come out of anywhere, and industry has often happened to be a good source! But “you are not solving a practical problem” is not a valid criticism of TCS, much like “you are not building fridges” is not a damning indictment of thermodynamics.

  3. We are meant to create knowledge, but that means disseminating it. The license society gives us for our curiosity-driven endeavours and theory building comes with a price:6 we need to then explain this knowledge, communicate and teach it to our peers, our research community, our graduate students, and have it percolate through our teaching for it to reach as many people as possible. Knowledge creation without efforts towards exposition and dissemination is just a self-centered endeavour, with no benefit to the research community or society, and no place in academia.

And if you’re wondering where to have these discussions, and how to be able to debate and exchange ideas in a fragmented world, I have good news (or at least a suggestion): StackExchange! CSTheory.SE (https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/) exists; it can be used; let’s use it!

That was the first point. The second one, equally important: what can we do to make things work for our students, postdocs, and the new generation? Again, I don’t have answers, just one big suggestion: let’s shield them during this chaotic transition.

(2) Look at whatever grant you have, or can apply for, put funding together, call every possible philanthropist or funding body you can, be creative: let’s offer as many 2-, 3-, 4-year fellowships, postdoc, or early-career researchers positions as possible for juniors to weather the storm.

Let me be clear: if you are tenured (or have a similarly stable position), now is not the time for hand-wringing. But a 3-year postdoc position which includes part-time teaching (assuming, as I do, that great teaching and exposition will always be in demand) or some side industry experience? This could make the difference between a promising researcher leaving the field, or managing to make it through and adapt to the changes our discipline is going through. A small endowment from some startup or industry? This could tip the scales and provide stability just for the few months a PhD student needs before landing a job they want. So now is the time to try our very best, and, without publicly lamenting the end of our field (or, worse, rejoicing in it), to silently do whatever we can to so that things work out for the new generation.

And of course, do take me up on it. I’ll be trying, too (if I don’t, you know where to find me. There’s probably a very short flight from where you are to Sydney, and my office is always open.)

Thanks to Sepehr Assadi, Sasho Nikolov, and Omer Reingold for very helpful feedback on earlier versions of this post.

  1. Some good ones, too. ↩

  2. If you haven’t, go read his post on the Theory Dish: https://theorydish.blog/2026/09/29/speeding-up-the-process-of-mourning/. ↩

  3. And a blog post by Lance Fortnow providing some context and perspective here: https://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/2016/06/karp-v-wigderson-20-years-later.html. ↩

  4. As I said, I don’t have definite answers: if you threw a rock in the general direction of the TCS community, you’d likely hit someone (i) with slightly different opinions, (ii) looking furious about a recent bump on their head. ↩

  5. There is a counterpart, though: we should not “claim practical relevance” if there is none. We are not beholden to solving industry questions, but if we claim to do so it has to be true. Cake, eating, having it too! ↩

  6. It’s a small price, but one we tend not to focus on unfortunately. For several reasons, among which that it’s typically less explicitly asked of us, and while it does take a lot of time it comes with few incentives. ↩

By Hung Le

item.title:
TR26-248 | Breaking the Parity Barrier for Constant-Depth Circuits |
Nikolai Chukhin
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sparsification

A constant-depth circuit consists of AND and OR gates of unbounded fan-in, arranged in a constant number of layers, that read the input literals; for example, a depth-three circuit is an OR of CNFs or an AND of DNFs. The classical lower bound of Håstad (1989) states that every depth-$d$ circuit computing the parity function has $2^{\Omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ gates. This parity barrier stood for decades: no explicit function was known to require depth-$d$ circuits of size $2^{\omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ for any constant $d$. OpenAI (2026) recently announced that they broke this barrier for depth-three circuits: they gave an explicit function in P that requires OR-AND-OR circuits of size $2^{\omega(\sqrt{n})}$. In this paper, we break the parity barrier at every constant depth with a simpler function. We prove that for every fixed $d \ge 3$, every depth-$d$ circuit computing the trilinear function $\sum_{i,j} a_{i+j} x_i y_j \bmod 2$ for $x,y \in \{0,1\}^n$ and $a \in \{0,1\}^{2n-1}$, requires $2^{\Omega((n\log n/\log\log n)^{1/(d-1)})}$ gates. Our proof combines the restriction lemma of OpenAI, for which we give a short new proof, with Håstad's switching lemma and the sparsification lemma of Calabro, Impagliazzo, and Paturi (2006).

item.title: Simultaneous Competitive and Regret Guarantees for TCP Acknowledgment
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Tsubasa Harada, Yasushi Kawase, Hanna Sumita

We study simultaneous competitive and regret guarantees for TCP acknowledgment. Each acknowledgment serves all pending packets, and the objective is to minimize the total acknowledgment and waiting costs. It is well known that no deterministic online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio better than $2$. Given $k$ randomized online experts and $0<\varepsilon<1$, we construct a randomized online algorithm whose realized total cost is always at most $(2+\varepsilon)$ times the offline optimal cost $\mathrm{OPT}$ and whose expected regret against the expert with the smallest realized cost is $O(\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}\log(k+1)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The algorithm requires no advance knowledge of the number of packets or $\mathrm{OPT}$. Our algorithm controls switching costs between experts and uses the gap between the permitted competitive bound and its current cost to determine when to learn. We also prove lower bounds showing that, for $k\ge 2$, this regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $\mathrm{OPT}$, $k$, and $\varepsilon$, and that $\varepsilon>0$ is necessary for sublinear regret.

item.title: Breaking Two Barriers for Dynamic Planar Reachability
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sparsification

Authors: Adam Karczmarz, Michał Włodarczyk

We consider the reachability problem in fully dynamic directed planar graphs: the graph undergoes edge updates (insertions and deletions) and we receive queries asking if one vertex is reachable from another. The current-best online algorithm for dynamic planar reachability spends worst-case time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$ per query/update [Subramanian, ESA '93]. This can be improved to $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2})$ in the offline setting or when the embedding is fixed [Diks and Sankowski, ESA '07]. Our contribution is twofold: 1. We present the first algorithm that breaks the square-root barrier for dynamic planar reachability in the offline setting, obtaining time ${O}(n^{0.49})$ per query/update. This shows that the problem is easier than answering distance queries in a dynamic undirected planar graph, for which a conditional lower bound of $n^{1/2 - o(1)}$ is known [Abboud and Dahlgaard, FOCS '16]. Notably, this lower bound applies to both online and offline algorithms. 2. Second, in the general online setting we design a randomized data structure with amortized update and query time ${O}(n^{0.664})$. This is the first improvement upon the exponent $2/3$ in over three decades. The main engine behind our theorems is a new sparsification framework aimed at maintaining information about reachability. Specifically, we study digraphs through the lens of VC dimensionality of certain set systems. First, we design sparse reachability emulators for planar digraphs that preserve the VC dimension. Second, we utilize orderings with a low ``stabbing number'' [Chazelle and Welzl, Discrete Comput. Geom. '89] to compute subquadratic reachability emulators in subquadratic time whenever the VC dimension is bounded.

item.title: The Matching Number Characterizes the Query Complexity of Edge Counting and Degree Moment Estimation
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Chenglin Fan, Wonseok Shin

Consider an unknown graph $G = (V,E)$ with vertex degrees $d_v$, accessed only by sampling uniformly random edges and querying the degrees of their endpoints. We study the query complexity of estimating the number of edges $m$ and the degree moments $M_s = \sum_{v \in V} (d_v)^s$ for fixed integers $s \ge 2$. In this model, [Beretta and Tětek, TALG 2024] estimate $m$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2+\sqrt n/\varepsilon)$ expected queries without knowing the number of vertices $n$, and [Bhattacharya and Pradhan, CIAC 2025] estimate $M_s$ using $O(n^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries when $n$ is given. We show that the query complexity of both problems is governed by the matching number $ν$ of $G$ (the maximum number of pairwise disjoint edges) rather than the number of vertices $n$, and that the dependence on $\varepsilon$ for degree moments can be polynomially improved. Our algorithms rest on a simple observation: the endpoints of a maximum matching cover every edge, so a random endpoint of a random edge falls on this set of $2ν$ vertices with probability at least $1/2$. For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, we give advice-free algorithms that estimate $m$ and $M_s$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$, without knowledge of $n$, $ν$, or other graph parameters. Specifically, our algorithms use $O(\min\{ν/\varepsilon, 1/\varepsilon^2+\sqrtν/\varepsilon\})$ expected queries for $m$ and $O(\min\{ν^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^{2/s}, ν^{1-1/(2s-1)}/\varepsilon^{2/(2s-1)}\})$ for $M_s$. Finally, our lower bounds show that for every $k \ge 2$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, these query complexities are optimal up to constant factors over graphs with matching number at most $k$.

item.title: QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Édouard Bonnet, Yeonsu Chang

A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvořák, EJC 2018; Dvořák and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding particular induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czyżewska et al., arXiv 2026].

item.title: Distributed $(Δ+1)$-Coloring in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ Rounds
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local computation

Authors: Marc Fuchs, Fabian Kuhn

We give a deterministic distributed algorithm for $(Δ+1)$-coloring an $n$-node graph of maximum degree $Δ$ in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds in both the LOCAL and CONGEST models. More generally, $(°+1)$-list coloring with lists from a color space of size $C\geqΔ+1$ can be solved in $O(\sqrtΔ\log(1+C/Δ)+\log^* n)$ rounds; in CONGEST, we assume $C\leq n^{O(1)}$. The algorithm combines Barenboim's polynomial coloring procedure with arbdefective decompositions, degree reduction, and a short family of hash functions. Using the polynomial procedure in the degree-reduction framework already gives an $O(\sqrtΔ\logΔ+\log^* n)$-round algorithm when $C=O(Δ)$. Hashing adapts the color space to the current degree and removes the logarithmic factor. We prove the existence of the hash family by the probabilistic method and compute it by deterministic exhaustive search, using unrestricted local computation. We also give an explicit variant based on lossless expanders that avoids this search and achieves $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds for $C=O(Δ)$.

item.title: Dynamic Maximal Independent Set using Predictions
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: insertion-only

Authors: Shahbaz Khan, Anshul Kumar

We present the first dynamic maximal independent set (MIS) of a graph with $n$ vertices and up to $m$ edges under edge updates in the prediction model, where a predicted update sequence is available for offline preprocessing before the real updates arrive online. We consider the incremental (insertion-only), decremental (deletions-only), and fully dynamic (insertions and deletions) models. Without predictions, deterministic algorithms need worst-case update time of $O(n)$ for decremental and $O(m)$ for incremental and fully dynamic settings. Bernstein et al.~[SODA26] proved under the combinatorial BMM conjecture, combinatorial incremental algorithms against an adaptive adversary require $Ω(n^{1-o(1)})$ amortized update time. We present deterministic incremental, decremental, and fully dynamic algorithms whose update times depend on the prediction error. This error is measured by the number $η_e$ of mispredicted updates, and by the number $η_v$ and total degree $η_v^*$ of vertices whose MIS membership was mispredicted. With $O(mn)$ preprocessing, our decremental and incremental algorithms achieve worst-case update times $O(η_v)$ and $O(η_e+η_v^*)$, respectively. Our fully dynamic algorithm achieves $O(η_e+η_v^*)$ worst-case update time with $O(un)$ preprocessing for $u$ updates. We also give space-efficient variants using $O(m)$ space for the decremental and $O(m\sqrt{m})$ for the incremental setting, at the cost of a logarithmic overhead in worst-case update time. Our algorithms satisfy consistency, robustness, and smooth degradation, the required properties of algorithms with predictions. They can also utilize the general error correction framework of Khan et al.~[Arxiv26], relaxing the error measures from first point of difference to prefix matching (for partially dynamic) and set edit distance (for fully dynamic), maintaining the same bounds.

item.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part I: Glauber Dynamics
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Aniket Das, Tselil Schramm

In the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem, we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\{\pm1\}^N$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. We show that Glauber dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization, demonstrating that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

item.title: LOCAL LLL in $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$ Rounds
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Maxime Flin, Mohsen Ghaffari, Magnús M. Halldórsson, Yannic Maus, Alexandre Nolin

We provide a $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$-round randomized LOCAL algorithm for the constructive Lovász Local Lemma with polynomial criterion $pd^{c} < 1$, for a sufficiently large constant $c$. The best previous general round complexity was $\widetilde O(\log n)$. The key ingredient is a local reduction that amplifies the LLL probability exponent quadratically, while increasing the dependency radius only by a constant factor.

item.title: A Fixed Parameter Sublinear Time Approximation Scheme for Metric Min-Sum Clustering
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Karthik C. S., Euiwoong Lee, Yuval Rabani, Chris Schwiegelshohn, Samson Zhou

Metric $k$-minsum clustering is a simple, natural, appealing density-based clustering criterion whose computational complexity remains poorly understood, despite the progress achieved fornother clustering criteria in the past three decades. In this paper we give an efficient approximation scheme for this problem that runs in sublinear time for mildly increasing $k$, and thus is fixed parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$. We complement this result by showing that similar algorithms are unlikely to exist for the closely related problems $k$-median and balanced $k$-median, assuming popular fine-grained complexity conjectures. Specifically, we show that no sublinear time algorithm with small approximation factors can exist even for $2$-median and balanced $2$-median. It was previously known that no efficient PTAS can exist for $k$-median and our results show a strong and perhaps surprising separation between the $k$-minsum clustering problem and $k$-median even in the sublinear regime. Our upper bounds improve qualitatively upon decades old results. Our lower bounds establish the first use of the Distributed PCP framework to clustering problems.

item.title: No Truly Sublogarithmic-Round Algorithm for Distributed MIS in the LOCAL Model
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Seri Khoury, Aaron Schild

We prove that $o(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})$-round randomized LOCAL algorithms find a maximal independent set (MIS) with subconstant probability on some input. This shows that the 40-year-old $O(\log n)$-round randomized CONGEST algorithm of Luby and Alon, Babai, and Itai is nearly optimal. Our lower bound improves upon the $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$-round lower bound of Khoury and Schild and nearly closes the 20+ year-old gap between the $O(\log n)$-round algorithm and the $Ω(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$-round lower bound of Kuhn, Moscibroda, and Wattenhofer. To close this gap, one must show a lower bound for a graph that is not locally treelike. We do this by starting with a $D$-regular, $Θ(\log_D n)$-girth graph, with $D = Θ(\log n)$. Crucially, this is not our final graph. We obtain our hard instance by \emph{replacing} each vertex of this treelike graph with a clique on $n^c$ vertices for some constant $c \in (0,1)$. We then replace each edge with a bipartite Erdős--Rényi graph between the corresponding cliques, with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$. We analyze arbitrary LOCAL algorithms on our non-treelike hard instance with a novel round elimination approach. We describe algorithms that output a set of vertices in this graph using two metrics: their \emph{occupancy probability} and their \emph{conflict probability}. Our round elimination framework takes an $r$-round algorithm and produces an $(r-1)$-round algorithm where occupancy and conflict probabilities collectively slightly degrade, but individually can significantly improve or degrade. This round elimination result is obtained by exploiting the lack of large biclique complements in dense bipartite Erdős--Rényi graphs, which in turn allows us to bound the entropy of the output distribution for any independent set algorithm.

item.title: Almost Optimal Relative Error Streaming Quantiles with Full Mergeability
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Tomáš Domes, Pavel Veselý

Quantile summaries provide a scalable way to estimate the distribution of individual attributes in large datasets that are often distributed across multiple machines or generated by sensor networks. The state-of-the-art summaries with \emph{relative error guarantees} of $\pm \varepsilon\cdot \mathrm{rank}$, offering increasingly higher accuracy towards the distribution's tails, are ReqSketch (Cormode et al., JACM 2023) and the recent streaming algorithm by Gribelyuk et al. (SODA 2025). For inputs of size $N$ and probability $δ$ of exceeding the error bound, ReqSketch achieves space of $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log^{1.5}(\varepsilon N)\cdot \sqrt{\log δ^{-1}})$ memory words, and offers \emph{full mergeability}, allowing distributed or parallel processing of datasets. In contrast, the latter algorithm exceeds the lower bound of $Ω(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N)\cdot \log\logδ^{-1})$ from (Cormode \& Veselý, PODS 2020) only by a factor of $O(\log\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log\log N)\cdot\log^2\logδ^{-1})$, but it lacks the mergeability property, is substantially more involved than ReqSketch, and has unclear practical performance. Both of these data structures consist of relative compactors from ReqSketch that subsample the stream in a structured way and work well in the streaming setting but are difficult to analyze under mergeability. We design a new relative-error quantile summary that achieves full mergeability and also improves the state-of-the-art streaming space bound to $$O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N) \cdot\log \log δ^{-1} \cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log \log(\varepsilon N) + \log \log δ^{-1})),$$ which is substantially closer to the lower bound. At the same time, our data structure is simpler than the algorithm from (Gribelyuk et al., SODA 2025) and therefore more suitable for implementation.

item.title: Sublinear-Time and Semi-Streaming Algorithms for Path Cover and TSP
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Sharareh Alipour, Ali Nowzari

We give improved sublinear-time and semi-streaming approximation algorithms for maximum path cover, $(1,2)$-TSP, and Max-TSP. For each fixed $\eps>0$, our distance-query algorithm estimates the optimum cost of an $n$-vertex $(1,2)$-TSP instance from above within factor $2-\cstar+\eps=1.413184\ldots+\eps$, with high probability, in $n^{2-Ω_\eps(1)}$ time, where $\cstar=2(\sec1-\tan1)$. This improves the $3/2+\eps$ factor of direct matching estimation in this subquadratic regime~\cite{BhattacharyaKissSaranurak2023} and of the faster near-linear estimator~\cite{BehnezhadEtAl2024}. A single random vertex order defines an implicit bipartite graph whose matchings project to path covers. An alternating-permutation analysis shows that its expected maximum matching size is at least $\cstar$ times the optimum path-cover size. On long paths, even the best of polynomially many uniform orders retains only a $\cstar+o(1)$ fraction with high probability. In semi-streaming, we construct deterministic $(5/7-\eps)$-approximate unweighted path covers and $(9/7+\eps+5/(7n))$-approximate $(1,2)$-TSP tours, improving the respective $2/3-\eps$ and $4/3+\eps+1/n$ guarantees in~\cite{AlipourFarokhnejadMoemke2025}. For nonnegative weights, we obtain $2/3-\eps$ for path cover and Max-TSP, improving the earlier asymptotic $7/12-\eps$ Max-TSP bound. These algorithms use $\poly(1/\eps)$ passes independent of $n$ and $O(n\log(n/\eps)\poly(1/\eps))$ words. We compute two approximate matchings separated by edge deletion. A cycle-compensation lemma accounts for the weight removed when breaking their cycles. For unweighted graphs, a third approximate matching on a simple auxiliary graph with at most $2n$ vertices chooses component connections; a Tutte--Berge count proves the stronger bound.

item.title: Semi-Streaming Estimation of the Held--Karp Bound and Graph-Metric TSP Cost
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: graph stream

Authors: Sharareh Alipour

The Held--Karp bound is a linear-programming lower bound for the metric traveling salesperson problem (TSP). We approximate this bound in the multi-pass insertion-only streaming model for metrics induced by connected positive-weight graphs. For an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graph and $0<\eps\le1/2$, the algorithm returns a $(1+\eps)$ upper approximation with high probability, using $\wtO(\eps^{-4})$ passes, $\wtO(n\eps^{-2})$ words, and $\wtO(m\eps^{-4})$ arithmetic operations per pass. We replace the changing edge-weight vector by a short history of multiplicative-weights (MWU) updates. After initialization, updates repeat until a column is removed. We store each repeated update once, with its repetition count. The record length depends on the number of columns, not updates; the argument applies to any fixed nonnegative matrix. For Held--Karp, tree-path queries recover edge weights from these records. Separate search and update thresholds allow fresh sparsifiers at successive search stages. Controlled rounding gives a bounded-precision implementation. The estimate yields a $(3/2+\eps)$ graph-metric TSP value estimate and a $(7/5+\eps)$ estimate when the input graph is unweighted. Conversely, in weighted graph streams, every one-pass $(1+η)$ upper approximation to Held--Karp, for fixed $0\leη<1$, requires quadratic space. The algorithms estimate values; they do not construct tours within these bounds.

item.title: Query Complexity of Densest Sub(hyper)graph Problems
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Sinan G. Aksoy, Eli Friedman, Nate Veldt, Stephen J. Young

Rubinstein et al. introduce the study of connectivity and minimum cut problems in the cut query model, where an algorithm can only access the edges of a graph through CUT queries. In this work, we examine the query complexity of densest subgraph problems. Our first contribution is to generalize the uniform sparsification approach for Densest Subgraph and other heavy subgraph problems to weighted graphs, achieving the following results. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Densest Subgraph in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, roughly matching the $Ω(n/\log n)$ lower bound we prove for randomized algorithms. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Max Cut in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. This improves upon the bound of $O(n\log^3 n(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2))$ queries achieved by Plevrakis et al., making significant progress towards their lower bound of $Ω(n/\log n)$ queries. In contrast, we rule out approximation schemes with truly subquadratic query complexity for Densest $k$-Subgraph and settle its exact query complexity in both the unweighted and deterministic settings. For hypergraphs, we show CUT queries alone cannot achieve $o(\sqrt{n})$-approximation for Densest Subhypergraph or $o(n)$-approximation for Densest $k$-Subhypergraph, regardless of the number of queries. Augmenting CUT queries with the EDGE oracle of Chen et al., we overcome this barrier for Densest Subhypergraph and obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation on rank-$r$ hypergraphs using $O(nr\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We also extend our Densest $k$-Subgraph hardness results to hypergraphs and prove exponential query lower bounds for exact Densest $k$-Subhypergraph. Lastly, confirming a conjecture of Chakrabarty and Liao, we show that simulating an ADD query using CUT and IS-EDGE$^?$ queries requires exponentially-many queries.

item.title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Shravan Mehra, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Vihan Shah

We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation. For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching. We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

item.title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Antoine Amarilli, Mikaël Monet, Harshul Sagar

We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems: - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$. - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known. - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$. - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.
